content:
The Lean Community website has a page on the Freek Wiedijk's 1000+ theorems project, which is a list of 1000+ theorems that the community wants formalized in Lean. If a group of people create a proof (or nearly complete proof) of one of the theorems, would it help to provide a GitHub link on the website so that other people can reference it? Alternatively, it may be helpful to have some way of indicating whether someone is developing a formalization for a larger library.

One of the pages on the website references a "database", but it isn't clear where this database is. Additionally, not all of the theorems will end up on MathLib (such as if CSLib or another library chooses to formalize it first), which makes the instructions for how to contribute theorems on the main page for the project confusing. Additionally, if a group in the community makes a formalization of a proof, it may not have the level of detail and generality needed to be put onto MathLib.

Part of my reasoning is that a group may want to formalize one of these missing theorems as a way to contribute to the community. Here are a couple reasons that are relevant to these groups:

  • If a theorem is planned to be implemented into a larger library soon, it helps to indicate this so that these groups don't accidentally work on something already being worked on.
  • Similarly, having two groups work on the same theorem could lead to overlapping work, though there is some benefit toward having multiple approaches. (See below)
  • If a group works on a formalization, it can feel sad to not have anywhere to indicate that work, especially if the group wanted to formalize it specifically so that it can contribute to the 1000+ Theorems list. While their work may not be directly added to a library, it may serve as inspiration for someone who is formalizing it for a library.
    • If multiple groups provide multiple approaches to a theorem, it can be more likely that one of the groups takes an approach that is helpful to those who are formalizing the theorems for a library.
  • If a formalization is nearly complete but is missing a hypothesis, it can't be implemented in any library until the hypothesis is proven. Adding this work to the list helps convey the fact that a hypothesis is missing and allows for others to contribute a formalization of the missing hypothesis. For example, I am working on a proof of Jacobi's Four-Square theorem that is largely about rearranging terms in a long calculation, but I won't be able to prove the Jacobi Triple Product formula over C\mathbb{C}C that I need.
  • Some groups may want to reprove a theorem that is listed—such as for learning, enjoyment, etc.—and having a reference can be helpful.

I can also understand if the 1000+ theorems list is mostly meant for library developers, but it would be helpful to indicate this intent on the website to avoid confusion. What are your thoughts on these points?

The website is generated from https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/docs/1000.yaml, which one can PR their work to.
I have put link to my github repo to the file, though I do have a self-rule that I would only PR a complete (and cleaned up if it was AI generated) formalization.
I wonder if it be a good idea to create a more casual forum/wiki page aside from the file, so one doesn't feel the need to have a complete work and can post status about their progress freely

Weiyi Wang said:

I wonder if it be a good idea to create a more casual forum/wiki page aside from the file, so one doesn't feel the need to have a complete work and can post status about their progress freely

If there's stuff to document about a specific problem then you can open an issue, see #mathlib4 > TODO lists @ 💬

@Danny Just to be clear: the 1000+ theorems page does accept entries from outside Mathlib. You mentioned CSLib, so see Q1308502 as an example, which was added exactly for the reason you mention of preventing duplicate work. Mathlib declarations are better supported, in that they more directly link to the docs/github, which I think is natural given that this is generated from a YAML file hosted in Mathlib and there are only ~30 entries from external repos.

You could certainly implement a more repo-agnostic version of this outside Mathlib, and there's also now the new wikidata attribute (see file#Mathlib/Tactic/CrossRefAttribute) that could be used instead of a YAML file, though this needs some work to include author information. Anyone should be able to experiment with setting this up! I just don't think it's been a high-priority feature.

I think I understand how it's meant to work now? mathlib has a list of the 1000+ theorems, so if we want to add something to the list, we make a pull request to mathlib to add info about our project, not to add our project's theorems to the MathLib library. I'll keep this in mind for when I'm ready to share my work.

If I'm making a project that I don't plan to upload to MathLib, should I still post to #mathlib4 > TODO lists @ 💬? I suppose it makes sense since I would be requesting for MathLib to prove a particular theorem. I happen to have ran into a commit relating to adding the Pentagonal Number Theorem, which is a lemma for the Jacobi Triple Product formula that I will need. I could request for the Jacobi Triple Product there.

Am I understanding everything correctly? I'm always anxious about doing things the wrong way...
